name: Quadrille
description: Quadrille is a four-player trick-taking game adapted from the Spanish Ombre. The winner of the bidding becomes Hombre, names trump, and may call a King for a partner. The declarer aims to win six of ten tricks using a 40-card pack with inverted red-suit ranking and special matadors (Spadille, Manille, Basta).

overview.description: Quadrille is a four-player trick-taking game adapted from the Spanish Ombre. The winner of the bidding becomes Hombre, names trump, and may call a King for a partner. The declarer aims to win six of ten tricks using a 40-card pack with inverted red-suit ranking and special matadors (Spadille, Manille, Basta).

history.origins: Quadrille was introduced to the southern provinces of France around 1695 and shortly thereafter to Paris. It is an adaptation of the three-player Spanish game Ombre (Hombre) for four players. First English rules appeared in The Game of Quadrille; or Ombre by Four (1720), described as 'the favourite game at the French Court.'
timeline: ca. 1695: Quadrille introduced in southern France.
Early 18th century: Spread to Paris and Britain; French rules published (1724).
1720sâ€“1820s: Dominant card game at the French court and among British nobility; notably popular with women.
1813: Referenced in Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice (Lady Catherine de Bourgh).
Mid-19th century: Declined in fashion, superseded by Whist and Boston.
Present: Almost forgotten; still played in West Friesland and by enthusiasts.
history.cultural: Was 'to the good taste of the French nation' and particularly favoured by women. Charles Lamb contrasted its 'chance-started, capricious, ever fluctuating alliances' with the steady antipathies of Whist. Frequently mentioned in 18thâ€“19th century literature and diaries.
history.evolution: Emerged as Ombre adapted for four players with variable partnerships (calling a King). Complex matador and ranking system preserved from Ombre. Influenced Boston Whist and Solo Whist. Mediateur (Mediator) was a later elaboration with additional bids.

setup.players: 4 players. Each plays for herself; temporary alliances form per deal via the called King.
setup.deck: 40 cards: A, K, Q, J, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 in each suit (8s, 9s, 10s removed).
setup.dealing: 1. Dealer shuffles; pone cuts. 2. Deal 10 cards each in batches of 4-3-3, 3-4-3, or 3-3-4. 3. Deal and play rotate right (counterclockwise).
setup.equipment: 40-card pack, counters or chips for stakes, score sheet.

rules.objective: As Hombre (declarer), win at least six of the ten tricks, either alone (Solo) or with a partner (Alliance). Opponents aim to prevent this.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Stakes**: Each player antes to the pool (or dealer antes four). 2. **Auction**: Eldest opens; players bid or pass in ascending order: Solo, Casco (with both black Aces), Dimidiator (exchange with called King), Alliance (call a King for partner). If all pass, Forced Spadille: holder of Spadille becomes Hombre and calls a King. 3. **Trump**: Hombre names trump (or partner may in Forced Spadille). 4. **Play**: Eldest leads. Must follow suit; may play any card if void. Highest trump wins, else highest of led suit. Spadille, Manille, Basta may be held back when trumps are led (unless a higher trump is led). 5. **Settlement**: Hombre wins or loses; pool and premiums paid accordingly.
keyRules: Spadille (Ace of Spades) is always the highest trump.
Basta (Ace of Clubs) is always the third highest trump.
Manille = lowest card of trump suit (2 in black suits, 7 in red suits); always second highest trump.
Red suits (plain): K > Q > J > A > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5 > 6 > 7. Black suits (plain): K > Q > J > 7 > 6 > 5 > 4 > 3 > 2.
Alliance: Hombre calls a non-trump King; holder is secret partner until the called card is played.
Forced Spadille: No vole; Hombre and partner aim for six tricks.

strategy.basic: Bid Alliance when you have a strong hand but need support; bid Solo when you can likely take six tricks alone. Call a King you do not hold to find a partner.
strategy.intermediate: Lead to weaken opponents' trumps; use Matadors (Spadille, Manille, Basta) to control key tricks. In Alliance, signal to partner through card play.
strategy.advanced: The privilege of holding back Matadors when trumps are led allows tactical delay. Sequence your plays to maximize trump pulls. As defender, coordinate to deny Hombre a sixth trick.
tips: Red-suit inversion affects discard and lead choices.
In Forced Spadille, the called partner's identity is secretâ€”avoid revealing through early play.
Premiers bonus rewards taking six tricks before opponents take one.

scoring.description: Stake-based. Hombre wins: takes pool and premiums (Solo, Matadors, Premiers). Hombre loses: Remise (5 tricks) = double pool; Codille (4 or fewer) = stiffer penalty. Bonuses: Premiers (six tricks before opponents take one), Matadors (top trumps held).
scoring.winCondition: Hombre (or Hombre's team) wins by taking six or more tricks. Loses with five (Remise) or four or fewer (Codille).

synthesis.shortDescription: 18th-century four-player trick-taking game: Hombre calls a King, names trump, aims for six tricks.
